epistemicBoundary.purpose: GDF1-A target/term separation and boundary corpus; this is not a frozen ontology or human motor-neuroscience model
doesNotProve: that one performance metric is Skill
that subjective embodiment follows objective control
that synthetic control implies human motor skill or PlayExperience

separations.reason: intent is participant-side meaning/desired distinction; input is observable interface evidence
raw events may be filtered, scaled, aggregated, interpreted or remapped before controlling a system variable
continuous/discrete control values may realize one semantic action, while one action may require a trajectory of control values
semantic action identity and spatiotemporal realization are different; indirect/turn-based actions may have little participant motor trajectory
different trajectories can be goal-equivalent; similar trajectories can have different outcomes under world context
capability, legality, timing, collision, opponent/world interaction or admission can block/modify an attempt
successful execution does not guarantee the higher-level goal
participant causal control, classical system controllability and subjective control/agency are different targets
assistance and inference can raise/lower subjective agency independently from exact command execution
skill is a learned conditional capability/distribution; performance is an episode/sample under conditions
technique is a method/policy/coordination pattern; skill concerns capability to use/adapt methods effectively
declarative/world knowledge can support skill but does not guarantee execution/control capability
closeness to target and dispersion/repeatability can vary independently
time to initiate after a signal differs from placing/controlling action relative to a temporal target or dynamic state
task-relevant variables can be stable while redundant movement dimensions vary
affordance is actor-environment relational possibility, not actor capacity alone
a physically/relationally possible action may be disallowed by game authority; formal permission is not a Gibsonian affordance
actor/player belief can miss or invent possibilities
representation/signalling of possibility is not the possibility itself
the whole biological body is not identical to the limb, gaze, voice or BCI channel used to express control
physical human movement can control a cursor, avatar, vehicle, army, menu, policy or other locus
not every controlled locus represents the player as an in-world proxy
body/avatar synchronization and control are causal inputs but subjective ownership/agency/self-location are distinct outcomes
transient performance change, compensation or fatigue does not by itself establish retained/generalizable learning

pressure: high strategic skill with negligible motor execution demand
GameAction not identical to participant movement
continuous/discrete timing and trajectory matter
small mapping/dynamics changes can alter executable skill space
decision, technique, sequence execution, timing and opponent adaptation coexist
input complexity is not identical to strategic depth
kinematic accuracy/precision/speed are measurable at scale
motor trajectory metrics predict performance but do not exhaust Game skill
closed-loop visuomotor regulation and prediction matter
vehicle dynamics can function as controlled body/tool without humanoid avatar
temporal phase/error and anticipation dominate over spatial accuracy
reaction time alone cannot model timing skill
player GameAction can be a semantic order while unit movement is system-executed
motor authority is not required for strategic action causality
different human movements/controllers can realize the same GameAction
mapping changes reachable player action without changing game rule semantics
system can suppress/correct low-level commands while preserving higher-level intent
objective command share and subjective agency can diverge
control synchrony/fidelity can affect embodiment
embodiment components remain distinct from objective task success
GameAction may be caused without ordinary limb movement
motor movement cannot be a universal GameAction primitive
policy/execution competence can exist without a human body
synthetic performance does not establish human-like embodiment or PlayExperience
mapping can change to improve access/performance
unannounced adaptation can change what is being learned and attributed
different movement solutions can preserve task-relevant outcome
exact repeatability is not necessary for skilled control

externalAnchors.claim: optimal-feedback account allows variability in task-irrelevant/redundant dimensions while stabilizing task goals
force-field adaptation and aftereffects support learned predictive representation of dynamics
sensorimotor experiment supports use of an internal model/state prediction
stair-climbing affordance boundary scales with actor-environment/body relation rather than absolute geometry alone
aimed movement exhibits a systematic speed-accuracy relation; movement difficulty cannot be reduced to speed or accuracy alone
computer assistance that ignored erroneous commands could improve performance and reported sense of agency, dissociating raw command execution from subjective agency
body ownership and agency can be experimentally dissociated
large-scale Aim Lab data show long-horizon refinement of motor acuity and retention across voluntary practice
FPS aiming exhibits kinematic regularities comparable to standard sensorimotor tasks; spatial movement metrics predict task performance
action-game experience related to faster sensorimotor learning for consistent/predictable tracking structure rather than a blanket initial control advantage
skill transfer across environment speeds required recalibration of action timing; higher skill was associated with lower variability in timing/chunking measures
changing the physical control interface enabled substantially more stroke participants to direct the same software cursor/game control, demonstrating mapping/access separation
different degrees of avatar motion control altered embodiment measures in task-dependent ways; objective control and embodiment are related but not identical
